claim: RNase E (RNE) is the main endoribonuclease in Escherichia coli, known for its role in RNA processing and mRNA degradation.
source: RNase E (RNE) is the main endoribonuclease in Escherichia coli, known for its role in RNA processing and mRNA degradation (Mudd et al., 1990; Mackie, 2013; Hui et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Mudd et al., 1990; Mackie, 2013; Hui et al., 2014).

claim: RNase E is an essential protein in E. coli.
source: It is an essential protein (Apirion and Lassar, 1978; Babitzke and Kushner, 1991)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Apirion and Lassar, 1978; Babitzke and Kushner, 1991).

claim: Homologous proteins to RNase E are found across many bacterial species.
source: homologous proteins are found across many bacterial species (Carpousis, 2007; Aït-Bara and Carpousis, 2015; Mardle et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Carpousis, 2007; Aït-Bara and Carpousis, 2015; Mardle et al., 2019).

claim: The essentiality of RNase E stems from the N-terminal domain (NTD), or the catalytic domain.
source: The essentiality stems from the N-terminal domain (NTD), or the catalytic domain (Callaghan et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Callaghan et al., 2005).

claim: The NTD of RNase E is followed by a membrane-targeting sequence (MTS) and the C-terminal domain (CTD).
source: The NTD is followed by a membrane-targeting sequence (MTS) and the C-terminal domain (CTD), or macromolecular interaction domain (Mackie, 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Mackie, 2013).

claim: RhlB (a DEAD-box RNA helicase), PNPase (a 3′ → 5′ exonuclease), and enolase (a glycolytic enzyme) bind to the CTD to form the RNA degradosome complex.
source: where RhlB (a DEAD-box RNA helicase), PNPase (a 3′ → 5′ exonuclease), and enolase (a glycolytic enzyme) bind to form the RNA degradosome complex (Carpousis, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Carpousis, 2007).

claim: The MTS forms an amphipathic α helix, responsible for the localization of RNE on the inner membrane.
source: The MTS forms an amphipathic α helix, responsible for the localization of RNE on the inner membrane (Khemici et al., 2008; Strahl et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Khemici et al., 2008; Strahl et al., 2015).

claim: The membrane localization of RNE and the presence of the CTD are not essential in E. coli.
source: Interestingly, the membrane localization of RNE and the presence of the CTD are not essential in E. coli nor are they conserved across bacterial species, in contrast to the broad conservation of the NTD across bacteria as well as chloroplasts (Aït-Bara and Carpousis, 2015; Kaberdin et al., 1998; Lee and Cohen, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Aït-Bara and Carpousis, 2015; Kaberdin et al., 1998; Lee and Cohen, 2003).

claim: The membrane localization of RNE and the presence of the CTD are not conserved across bacterial species.
source: Interestingly, the membrane localization of RNE and the presence of the CTD are not essential in E. coli nor are they conserved across bacterial species, in contrast to the broad conservation of the NTD across bacteria as well as chloroplasts (Aït-Bara and Carpousis, 2015; Kaberdin et al., 1998; Lee and Cohen, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Aït-Bara and Carpousis, 2015; Kaberdin et al., 1998; Lee and Cohen, 2003).

claim: The NTD of RNase E is broadly conserved across bacteria as well as chloroplasts.
source: Interestingly, the membrane localization of RNE and the presence of the CTD are not essential in E. coli nor are they conserved across bacterial species, in contrast to the broad conservation of the NTD across bacteria as well as chloroplasts (Aït-Bara and Carpousis, 2015; Kaberdin et al., 1998; Lee and Cohen, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Aït-Bara and Carpousis, 2015; Kaberdin et al., 1998; Lee and Cohen, 2003).

claim: E. coli strains with cytoplasmic RNE (due to the removal of the MTS) are viable, although they grow more slowly than the wild-type (WT) cells.
source: E. coli strains with cytoplasmic RNE (due to the removal of the MTS) are viable, although they grow more slowly than the wild-type (WT) cells (Khemici et al., 2008; Hadjeras et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Khemici et al., 2008; Hadjeras et al., 2019).

claim: In vitro studies have shown that membrane binding of RNE does not necessarily increase its enzymatic activity.
source: In vitro studies have shown that membrane binding of RNE does not necessarily increase its enzymatic activity (Khemici et al., 2008; Hadjeras et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Khemici et al., 2008; Hadjeras et al., 2019).

claim: Membrane localization is likely important for gene regulation in vivo because RNE becomes sequestered from the cytoplasmic pool of mRNAs, giving mRNAs time for translation.
source: However, membrane localization is likely important for gene regulation in vivo because RNE becomes sequestered from the cytoplasmic pool of mRNAs, giving mRNAs time for translation.
evidence: The claim is presented as a logical inference based on the sequestration of RNE from cytoplasmic mRNAs.

claim: Membrane-bound RNE limits the degradation of nascent mRNAs while cytoplasmic RNE (ΔMTS) can degrade nascent mRNAs during transcription.
source: This idea is supported by our recent observation that the membrane-bound RNE limits the degradation of nascent mRNAs while cytoplasmic RNE (ΔMTS) can degrade nascent mRNAs during transcription (Kim et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent study (Kim et al., 2024).

claim: Transcripts encoding membrane proteins can experience co-transcriptional degradation assisted by the transertion effect.
source: We found that transcripts encoding membrane proteins can be an exception to this rule, in that they can experience co-transcriptional degradation assisted by the transertion effect (Kim et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent study (Kim et al., 2024).

claim: The membrane localization of RNE allows for differential regulation of mRNA stability for genes encoding cytoplasmic proteins versus inner membrane proteins in E. coli.
source: These findings agree with results from a genome-wide study, indicating that the membrane localization of RNE allows for differential regulation of mRNA stability for genes encoding cytoplasmic proteins versus inner membrane proteins in E. coli (Moffitt et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a genome-wide study (Moffitt et al., 2016).

claim: E. coli RNE can localize in the cytoplasm when cells were grown anaerobically.
source: Previous studies have reported evidence that E. coli RNE can localize in the cytoplasm—for example, when cells were grown anaerobically (Murashko and Lin-Chao, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Murashko and Lin-Chao, 2017).

claim: E. coli RNE can localize in the cytoplasm when membrane fluidity was reduced by changes in lipid composition.
source: or when membrane fluidity was reduced by changes in lipid composition (Gohrbandt et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Gohrbandt et al., 2022).

claim: RNE can dissociate from the membrane.
source: These findings imply that RNE can dissociate from the membrane; however, the origin of its weak membrane binding remains unknown.
evidence: The claim is inferred from previous findings showing cytoplasmic localization of RNE under certain conditions.

claim: Several species within α-proteobacteria have cytoplasmic RNE.
source: Across bacteria, several species within α-proteobacteria have cytoplasmic RNE (Al-Husini et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Al-Husini et al., 2018).

claim: B. subtilis RNase Y (a functional homolog of RNE) associates with the membrane via a transmembrane (TM) motif.
source: Among these, B. subtilis RNase Y (a functional homolog of RNE) associates with the membrane via a transmembrane (TM) motif (Lehnik-Habrink et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Lehnik-Habrink et al., 2011).

claim: E. coli and other γ-proteobacteria use an amphipathic motif for membrane association of RNE.
source: instead of an amphipathic motif used by E. coli and other γ-proteobacteria (Aït-Bara and Carpousis, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Aït-Bara and Carpousis, 2015).

claim: The CTD of E. coli RNE is an intrinsically disordered region.
source: Lastly, the CTD of E. coli RNE is an intrinsically disordered region (Callaghan et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Callaghan et al., 2004).

claim: The CTD of RNase E is nonessential for cell viability but enhances the enzymatic activity of the NTD.
source: that, while nonessential for cell viability, enhances the enzymatic activity of the NTD (Lopez et al., 1999; Leroy et al., 2002; Islam et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Lopez et al., 1999; Leroy et al., 2002; Islam et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2024).

claim: The CTD is the primary binding site for degradosome components.
source: As the primary binding site for degradosome components (Carpousis, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Carpousis, 2007).

claim: The CTD is thought to facilitate mRNA degradation by recruiting degradosome proteins near the catalytic NTD.
source: the CTD is thought to facilitate mRNA degradation by recruiting these proteins near the catalytic NTD.
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis based on the CTD's role as a binding site for degradosome components.

claim: Degradosome-associated proteins have minimal impact on the degradation rate of lacZ mRNA.
source: However, our recent study showed that these associated proteins have minimal impact on the degradation rate of lacZ mRNA, whereas deletion of the CTD markedly stabilizes the transcript (Kim et al., 2024)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent study (Kim et al., 2024).

claim: Deletion of the CTD markedly stabilizes lacZ mRNA transcript.
source: However, our recent study showed that these associated proteins have minimal impact on the degradation rate of lacZ mRNA, whereas deletion of the CTD markedly stabilizes the transcript (Kim et al., 2024)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent study (Kim et al., 2024).

claim: The CTD modulates the membrane-binding affinity of RNE, possibly by affecting its conformation.
source: In the present study, we further show that the CTD modulates the membrane-binding affinity of RNE, possibly by affecting its conformation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the current study, with a speculative mechanism proposed.

claim: ~93% of RNase E localizes to the inner membrane.
source: Super-resolution microscopy revealed that ~93% of RNase E localizes to the inner membrane and exhibits slow diffusion similar to polysomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RNase E exhibits slow diffusion similar to polysomes.
source: Super-resolution microscopy revealed that ~93% of RNase E localizes to the inner membrane and exhibits slow diffusion similar to polysomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The native amphipathic MTS confers slower diffusion compared to a transmembrane motif.
source: Comparing the native amphipathic MTS with a transmembrane motif showed that the MTS confers slower diffusion and stronger membrane binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The native amphipathic MTS confers stronger membrane binding compared to a transmembrane motif.
source: Comparing the native amphipathic MTS with a transmembrane motif showed that the MTS confers slower diffusion and stronger membrane binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The CTD slows diffusion of RNase E by increasing mass.
source: The CTD further slows diffusion by increasing mass but unexpectedly weakens membrane association.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing the effect of CTD on diffusion.

claim: The CTD unexpectedly weakens membrane association of RNase E.
source: The CTD further slows diffusion by increasing mass but unexpectedly weakens membrane association.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing the effect of CTD on membrane binding.

claim: RNase E mutants with partial cytoplasmic localization displayed enhanced co-transcriptional degradation of lacZ mRNA.
source: RNase E mutants with partial cytoplasmic localization displayed enhanced co-transcriptional degradation of lacZ mRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript on lacZ mRNA degradation rates.

claim: Previous fluorescence microscopy studies have shown that RNE is localized to the inner membrane in E. coli.
source: Previous fluorescence microscopy studies have shown that RNE is localized to the inner membrane in E. coli (Khemici et al., 2008; Strahl et al., 2015; Moffitt et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Khemici et al., 2008; Strahl et al., 2015; Moffitt et al., 2016).

claim: The percentage of membrane-bound RNase E molecules has not been quantitatively examined in live cells prior to this study.
source: but the percentage of membrane-bound molecules has not been quantitatively examined in live cells.
evidence: The claim is presented as a gap in the literature that this study addresses.

claim: RNE was fused with a photo-convertible fluorescent protein, mEos3.2, for imaging individual RNE molecules.
source: To address this gap, we fused RNE with a photo-convertible fluorescent protein, mEos3.2 (Zhang et al., 2012) and imaged individual RNE molecules over time in two dimensions (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Zhang et al., 2012) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The positions of fluorescent molecules were identified in each frame and linked into trajectories using the open-source software u-track.
source: The positions of fluorescent molecules were identified in each frame and linked into trajectories using the open-source software u-track (Jaqaman et al., 2008; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Jaqaman et al., 2008) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The MB% of LacY was 99% with a 95% confidence interval of [96%, 100%].
source: The MB% of LacY was 99% with a 95% confidence interval of [96%, 100%], and LacZ showed MB% of 3.4% [0.2%, 7.3%] (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1E and F.

claim: LacZ showed MB% of 3.4% [0.2%, 7.3%].
source: The MB% of LacY was 99% with a 95% confidence interval of [96%, 100%], and LacZ showed MB% of 3.4% [0.2%, 7.3%] (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1E and F.

claim: For RNE, the MB% was found to be 93% [91%, 96%].
source: For RNE, we found an MB% of 93% [91%, 96%] (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: The xNorm histogram of the fastest 7% of the RNE population exhibited a cytoplasmic localization pattern.
source: The xNorm histogram of the fastest 7% of the RNE population (based on the diffusion coefficient, as discussed below) exhibited a cytoplasmic localization pattern (without the two membrane-associated peaks), supporting the existence of a cytoplasmic RNE subpopulation (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The MTS (residues 568–582) is essential for the membrane binding of RNE.
source: We confirmed that the MTS (residues 568–582) is essential for the membrane binding of RNE, as deletion of the MTS sequence made the xNorm like that of LacZ (Figure 2A, B, Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2A, B, and Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The xNorm profile of RNE ΔMTS was slightly different from that of LacZ near the center line of the cell (x = 0), suggesting fewer RNE ΔMTS molecules were at the midline of the cell.
source: We note that the xNorm profile of RNE ΔMTS was slightly different from that of LacZ near the center line of the cell (x = 0), suggesting fewer RNE ΔMTS molecules were at the midline of the cell.
evidence: The claim is based on observation of xNorm profiles and inference about molecular distribution.

claim: xNorm fitting of RNE ΔMTS yielded an MB% of 33%.
source: Also, xNorm fitting yielded an MB% of 33%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The xNorm profile differences for RNE ΔMTS may reflect nucleoid exclusion of RNE ΔMTS due to its large size.
source: These results may reflect nucleoid exclusion of RNE ΔMTS due to its large size (Thappeta et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is presented as a possible explanation supported by a citation to a published study (Thappeta et al., 2024).

claim: A smaller cytoplasmic RNE variant generated by CTD truncation (RNE (1–529) or RNE ΔMTS ΔCTD) exhibited a xNorm profile closer to that of LacZ.
source: Consistently, a smaller cytoplasmic RNE variant generated by CTD truncation (RNE (1–529) or RNE ΔMTS ΔCTD) exhibited a xNorm profile closer to that of LacZ (Figure 2B, Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B and Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The MTS forms an amphipathic α-helix, in which hydrophobic residues are expected to align on one side of the helix.
source: The MTS forms an amphipathic α-helix, in which hydrophobic residues are expected to align on one side of the helix (Figure 2C; Khemici et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Khemici et al., 2008) and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Previous studies suggested that replacing one of the hydrophobic residues with a hydrophilic amino acid can disrupt membrane binding of RNE.
source: Previous studies suggested that replacing one of the hydrophobic residues with a hydrophilic amino acid can disrupt membrane binding of RNE (Khemici et al., 2008; Strahl et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Khemici et al., 2008; Strahl et al., 2015).

claim: The F574A F575A double mutation (noted as F574AA) did not significantly affect MB%.
source: We found that the F574A F575A double mutation (noted as F574AA) did not significantly affect MB%, consistent with the fact that the substituted amino acids remain hydrophobic (Figure 2D, E, Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2D, E, and Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: F582E and F575E mutations reduced MB% to 47% and 50%, respectively.
source: In contrast, F582E and F575E mutations reduced MB% to 47% and 50%, respectively (Figure 2E)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: The xNorm histograms of F582E and F575E mutations resembled that of RNE ΔMTS, suggesting predominantly cytoplasmic localization.
source: and their xNorm histograms resembled that of RNE ΔMTS, suggesting predominantly cytoplasmic localization (Figure 2D, Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2D and Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The phenylalanine residues at positions 575 and 582 are critical for membrane association of RNE.
source: These findings indicate that the phenylalanine residues at positions 575 and 582 are critical for membrane association of RNE.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced MB% with mutations at these positions.

claim: The diffusion coefficient D of RNE was calculated by fitting the mean-squared displacement (MSD) of each trajectory to the equation MSD = 4Dτ + b.
source: We calculated the diffusion coefficient D by fitting the mean-squared displacement (MSD) of each trajectory to the equation MSD = 4Dτ + b, where τ is lag time and b accounts for both dynamic and static localization errors (Savin and Doyle, 2005; Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Savin and Doyle, 2005) and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: DRNE was measured to be 0.0184 ± 0.0002 µm2/s.
source: We obtained DRNE = 0.0184 ± 0.0002 µm2/s (mean ± SEM, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lower detection limit of the microscope for diffusion was determined to be D = 0.0020 ± 0.0001 μm2/s using stationary, surface-immobilized mEos3.2.
source: This value was well above the lower detection limit of our microscope, determined using stationary, surface-immobilized mEos3.2, D = 0.0020 ± 0.0001 μm2/s (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: DRNE was comparable to that of ribosome-bound mRNAs, estimated to be D ~ 0.015 µm2/s based on the diffusion of ribosomal protein L1.
source: Notably, DRNE was comparable to that of ribosome-bound mRNAs, estimated to be D ~ 0.015 µm2/s based on the diffusion of ribosomal protein L1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: DΔMTS is ~5.5 times that of DRNE.
source: We found that DΔMTS is ~5.5 times that of DRNE (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Membrane-bound RNE (1–592) and cytoplasmic RNE (1–529) differ in D values by a factor of ~5.3 due to localization.
source: These truncated variants diffused faster than their full-length counterparts due to reduced mass, but their D values still differed by a factor of ~5.3 due to localization (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Membrane binding reduces RNE mobility by a factor of 5.
source: Together, these results suggest that the membrane binding reduces RNE mobility by a factor of 5.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparative diffusion data of membrane-bound and cytoplasmic RNE variants.

claim: In rif-treated cells, DRNE increased to 0.0270 ± 0.0003 µm2/s, which is 1.47 ± 0.010 times that in untreated cells.
source: In rif-treated cells, DRNE increased to 0.0270 ± 0.0003 µm2/s, which is 1.47 ± 0.010 times that in untreated cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: DLacY increased to 1.25 ± 0.01 times relative to untreated cells upon rifampicin treatment.
source: We note that DLacY also increased to 1.25 ± 0.01 times relative to untreated cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: The increase in DLacY upon rifampicin treatment likely results from the depletion of mRNAs near the membrane, which could otherwise hinder the diffusion of membrane proteins.
source: The increase in DLacY likely results from the depletion of mRNAs near the membrane (e.g., the mRNAs undergoing transertion), which could otherwise hinder the diffusion of membrane proteins (Binenbaum et al., 1999; Matsumoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is presented as a likely explanation supported by citations to two published studies (Binenbaum et al., 1999; Matsumoto et al., 2015).

claim: The similar fold change in DRNE and DLacY upon rif treatment suggests that the change in RNE diffusion may largely be attributed to physical changes in the intracellular environment rather than a loss of RNA–RNE interactions.
source: The similar fold change in DRNE and DLacY upon rif treatment suggests that the change in RNE diffusion may largely be attributed to physical changes in the intracellular environment (such as reduced viscosity or macromolecular crowding; Bellotto et al., 2022; Linnik et al., 2024), rather than a loss of RNA–RNE interactions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparative data and supported by citations to two published studies (Bellotto et al., 2022; Linnik et al., 2024).

claim: The diffusion of ribosomal protein L1 became seven times as fast in rif-treated cells.
source: The diffusion of ribosomal protein L1 became seven times as fast as that in rif-treated cells (Figure 3E)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: The large change in ribosomal protein L1 diffusion upon rifampicin treatment is consistent with previous reports.
source: consistent with previous reports (Sanamrad et al., 2014; Bakshi et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Sanamrad et al., 2014; Bakshi et al., 2012).

claim: The large change in ribosomal protein L1 diffusion can be explained by the fact that ribosomes form polysomes, where the effective mass of L1 protein in untreated cells would be 2 or more times that in rif-treated cells.
source: This big change can be explained by the fact that ribosomes form polysomes, where the effective mass of L1 protein in untreated cells would be 2 or more times that in rif-treated cells (where it remains as a free subunit).
evidence: The claim is presented as an explanation based on the known behavior of ribosomes forming polysomes.

claim: RNE forms the RNA degradosome complex, whose mass can be from 450 kDa to 2.3 MDa depending on the occupancy of the RNA degradosome component proteins.
source: In the case of RNE, it forms the RNA degradosome complex, whose mass can be from 450 kDa (Carpousis, 2007) to 2.3 MDa depending on the occupancy of the RNA degradosome component proteins (RhlB, PNPase, and enolase) (Chandran and Luisi, 2006; Chandran et al., 2007; Mackie, 2013; Nurmohamed et al., 2010; Nurmohamed et al., 2009) (see Appendix 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Carpousis, 2007; Chandran and Luisi, 2006; Chandran et al., 2007; Mackie, 2013; Nurmohamed et al., 2010; Nurmohamed et al., 2009).

claim: Even at its largest size, the RNE complex is smaller than a 70S ribosome (~2.5 MDa).
source: Even at its largest size, the RNE complex is smaller than a 70S ribosome (~2.5 MDa; Stark et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Stark et al., 1995).

claim: DRNE remained unchanged compared to untreated cells when cells were treated with chloramphenicol or when lacZ mRNA was overexpressed.
source: However, DRNE remained unchanged compared to untreated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The result that DRNE remained unchanged rules out the possibility that only a small percentage of RNE interacts with mRNAs and instead weighs in favor of the scenario that RNE–mRNA interactions are brief.
source: This result rules out the possibility that only a small percentage of RNE interacts with mRNAs and instead weighs in favor of the scenario that RNE–mRNA interactions are brief.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no change in DRNE under conditions expected to increase RNE-mRNA interactions.

claim: If RNE interacts with mRNAs for ~20 ms or less, the slow-diffusing state would last shorter than the frame interval and remain undetected in the experiment.
source: Specifically, if RNE interacts with mRNAs for ~20 ms or less, the slow-diffusing state would last shorter than the frame interval and remain undetected in our experiment.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculative explanation based on the experimental frame interval.

claim: RNase Y, a functional homolog of RNE in B. subtilis, is localized to the membrane via a TM domain.
source: Unlike RNE in E. coli, RNase Y, a functional homolog of RNE in B. subtilis, is localized to the membrane via a TM domain (Lehnik-Habrink et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Lehnik-Habrink et al., 2011).

claim: Both the MTS segment and LacY-derived TM segments showed a strong membrane enrichment.
source: Both the MTS segment and LacY-derived TM segments showed a strong membrane enrichment (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: LacY2 and LacY6 diffused faster than the MTS segment.
source: In terms of diffusion, LacY2 and LacY6 diffused faster than the MTS segment (Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: The diffusion of LacY2 and LacY6 being faster than the MTS segment is contrary to expectations based on size (or mass)-dependent diffusion.
source: contrary to expectations based on size (or mass)-dependent diffusion (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of diffusion data with expected size-dependent behavior shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The Saffman–Delbruck model predicts that D for membrane proteins decreases logarithmically with increasing radius of the membrane-embedded region.
source: Specifically, the Saffman–Delbruck model predicts that D for membrane proteins decreases logarithmically with increasing radius of the membrane-embedded region, assuming a constant membrane environment (Saffman and Delbrück, 1975).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Saffman and Delbrück, 1975).

claim: The observed discrepancy in diffusion implies that D may be governed by how each motif interacts with the membrane.
source: The observed discrepancy instead implies that D may be governed by how each motif interacts with the membrane.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that diffusion does not follow size-dependent expectations.

claim: All-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were conducted using the NAMD software.
source: To further explore this, we conducted all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the MTS and the LacY variants interacting with the E. coli membrane using the NAMD software (Phillips et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the NAMD software (Phillips et al., 2005).

claim: In MD simulations, the overall trends in diffusion were preserved; among the LacY series, larger constructs diffused more slowly.
source: Although the absolute D values were higher than experimental values (possibly due to the absence of mEos3.2 in the model), the overall trends were preserved; among the LacY series, larger constructs diffused more slowly (Figure 4E, F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4E, F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MTS diffused more slowly than LacY2 in silico.
source: Most importantly, the MTS again diffused more slowly than LacY2 in silico (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MTS–membrane interactions were more stable than those of LacY2.
source: By calculating membrane–protein interaction energies, we found that the MTS–membrane interactions were more stable than those of LacY2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The slower diffusion of the MTS is due to stronger interactions with lipid head groups compared to membrane-embedded TM segments.
source: These results suggest that the slower diffusion of the MTS is due to stronger interactions with lipid head groups compared to membrane-embedded TM segments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the MD simulation data showing stronger MTS-membrane interactions.

claim: All chimeric RNE mutants were expressed from the native chromosomal locus as the only copy of rne, with mEos3.2 fused at the C terminus for imaging.
source: All chimeric RNE mutants were expressed from the native chromosomal locus as the only copy of rne, with mEos3.2 fused at the C terminus for imaging.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design for expressing chimeric RNE mutants.

claim: The resulting strains expressing chimeric RNE mutants exhibited no noticeable differences in growth rate compared to the WT strain.
source: The resulting strains exhibited no noticeable differences in growth rate compared to the WT strain (Supplementary file 3), suggesting that the RNE mutants were functionally active.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Mutants containing the CTD showed noticeable cytoplasmic subpopulations when LacY2 and LacY6 were used in place of the MTS.
source: However, mutants containing the CTD showed noticeable cytoplasmic subpopulations when LacY2 and LacY6 were used in place of the MTS (Figure 5D, Appendix 1—figures 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5D and Appendix 1—figures 1 and 2.

claim: The MB% of RNE-LacY2-CTD was estimated to be 69% [66%, 73%].
source: Mathematical model fitting of the xNorm histograms estimated the MB% of RNE-LacY2-CTD and RNE-LacY6-CTD to be 69% [66%, 73%] and 86% [84%, 90%], respectively (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: The MB% of RNE-LacY6-CTD was estimated to be 86% [84%, 90%].
source: Mathematical model fitting of the xNorm histograms estimated the MB% of RNE-LacY2-CTD and RNE-LacY6-CTD to be 69% [66%, 73%] and 86% [84%, 90%], respectively (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Imperfect membrane localization was observed only in mutants containing the CTD; the same protein without the CTD showed MB% of 100%.
source: We note that imperfect membrane localization was observed only in mutants containing the CTD; the same protein without the CTD showed MB% of 100% (Figure 5E, F, Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5E, F, and Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The CTD may contribute to unstable membrane binding of RNE.
source: These findings suggest that the CTD may contribute to unstable membrane binding of RNE.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CTD-containing mutants show reduced MB%.

claim: Previously characterized RNE MTS point mutants with MB%<50% exhibited increased MB% upon the CTD removal.
source: Supporting this idea, previously characterized RNE MTS point mutants with MB%<50% (Figure 2D, E) also exhibited increased MB% upon the CTD removal (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2D, E, and Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The difference in MB% between the CTD-containing and the CTD-lacking mutants was not observed in the chimera based on LacY12.
source: Such a difference in MB% between the CTD-containing and the CTD-lacking mutants was not observed in the chimera based on LacY12 (Figure 5E, F), possibly due to the stable membrane insertion by LacY12.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5E, F, with a speculative explanation provided.

claim: In the absence of the CTD, the D of LacY2-based RNE was 1.33 ± 0.01 times as fast as the MTS-based RNE.
source: Indeed, in the absence of the CTD, we found that the D of LacY2-based RNE was 1.33 ± 0.01 times as fast as the MTS-based RNE (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5G.

claim: LacY6-based RNE did not diffuse faster than the MTS-based version.
source: However, LacY6-based RNE did not diffuse faster than the MTS-based version (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5G.

claim: The high TM load (24 helices) created by four LacY6 anchors in the RNE tetramer likely enlarges the membrane-embedded footprint and increases drag, thereby changing the mobility advantages.
source: This result may be due to the high TM load (24 helices) created by four LacY6 anchors in the RNE tetramer. Although all constructs are tetrameric, the 24-helix load (LacY6), compared with 8 (LacY2) and 4 (MTS), likely enlarges the membrane-embedded footprint and increases drag, thereby changing the mobility advantages assessed as standalone membrane anchors.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculative explanation for the observed diffusion behavior.

claim: In the presence of the CTD, the D of LacY2 and LacY6-based RNE became 3.33 ± 0.004 and 1.14 ± 0.01 times that of the MTS-based RNE counterpart (i.e., the WT RNE), respectively.
source: In the presence of the CTD, the D of LacY2 and LacY6-based RNE became 3.33 ± 0.004 and 1.14 ± 0.01 times that of the MTS-based RNE counterpart (i.e., the WT RNE), respectively (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5H.

claim: The increased diffusion of LacY2 and LacY6-based RNE in the presence of the CTD is likely influenced by the presence of a cytoplasmic population.
source: This is likely influenced by the presence of a cytoplasmic population (~31% for LacY2 and ~14% for LacY6; Figure 5F, Appendix 1—figure 2J), which diffuses more rapidly than membrane-bound molecules (possibly by a factor of five, based on Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data on MB% and diffusion presented in Figure 5F, Appendix 1—figure 2J, and Figure 3B.

claim: The CTD weakens the membrane association of RNE and small TM motifs can facilitate the diffusion of RNE.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that the CTD weakens the membrane association of RNE and small TM motifs can facilitate the diffusion of RNE.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective data on MB% and diffusion of various RNE mutants.

claim: In WT cells, the co-transcriptional degradation rate (kd1) is about 10 times slower than the post-transcriptional degradation rate (kd2).
source: In WT cells, we found that the co-transcriptional degradation rate (kd1) is about 10 times slower than the post-transcriptional degradation rate (kd2) (Kim et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent study (Kim et al., 2024).

claim: In cells expressing RNE ΔMTS, kd1 increases by a factor of ~3.
source: In cells expressing RNE ΔMTS, however, kd1 increases by a factor of ~3, suggesting that cytoplasmic RNE can freely diffuse and degrade nascent mRNAs (Kim et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent study (Kim et al., 2024).

claim: The relative abundances of 5′ lacZ mRNA (Z5) remained constant prior to the rise in 3′ lacZ mRNA (Z3) levels in WT cells, confirming negligible co-transcriptional degradation.
source: The relative abundances of 5′ lacZ mRNA (Z5) remained constant prior to the rise in 3′ lacZ mRNA (Z3) levels (between ~100 and 210 s), confirming negligible co-transcriptional degradation in WT cells (Kim et al., 2024; Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6A and a citation to a recent study (Kim et al., 2024).

claim: In cells expressing RNE-LacY2-CTD (MB% = 69%), Z5 levels exhibited a downward trend during the same time window.
source: However, in cells expressing RNE-LacY2-CTD (MB% = 69%), Z5 levels exhibited a downward trend during the same time window (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: The estimated kd1 for RNE-LacY2-CTD was close to what was observed in RNE ΔMTS.
source: The estimated kd1 was close to what was observed in RNE ΔMTS (Kim et al., 2024) (gray line, p = 0.28; Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6C and a citation to a recent study (Kim et al., 2024).

claim: A similarly high kd1 was observed in RNE MTS point mutations, F582E and F757E.
source: A similarly high kd1 was also observed in RNE MTS point mutations, F582E and F757E, which exhibited a ΔMTS-like xNorm profile (Figure 2D), supporting the idea that the cytoplasmic subpopulation of RNE enables co-transcriptional mRNA degradation in E. coli (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6C and Figure 2D.

claim: RNE-LacY6-CTD, which exhibited a cytoplasmic subpopulation (~14% from MB% of 86%), did not exhibit a significant increase in kd1.
source: Notably, RNE-LacY6-CTD, which also exhibited a cytoplasmic subpopulation (~14% from MB% of 86%), did not exhibit a significant increase in kd1 (Figure 6C)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: A critical amount of cytoplasmic population may be needed to facilitate co-transcriptional mRNA degradation.
source: suggesting a critical amount of cytoplasmic population may be needed to facilitate co-transcriptional mRNA degradation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RNE-LacY6-CTD with ~14% cytoplasmic population did not show increased kd1.

claim: kd2 did not significantly vary across membrane-targeting variants in the presence of the CTD.
source: In the presence of the CTD, kd2 did not significantly vary across membrane-targeting variants (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Even though the LacY12 motif slows RNE diffusion, its kd2 was similar to that of WT RNE.
source: For example, even though the LacY12 motif slows RNE diffusion, its kd2 was similar to that of WT RNE (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Overexpression of WT RNE does not significantly change kd1 or kd2.
source: We tested this explicitly and found that overexpression of WT RNE does not significantly change kd1 or kd2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: When the CTD is present, neither copy number nor diffusion of membrane-bound RNE limits kd2.
source: Thus, when the CTD is present, neither copy number nor diffusion of membrane-bound RNE limits kd2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing no significant variation in kd2 across variants and no effect of RNE overexpression.

claim: In the absence of the CTD, kd1 was high in RNE variant F582E (MB% = 67%), reaching levels close to its cytoplasmic counterpart, the ΔMTS ΔCTD mutant.
source: In the absence of the CTD, kd1 was high in RNE variant F582E (MB% = 67%; Appendix 1—figure 1), reaching levels close to its cytoplasmic counterpart, the ΔMTS ΔCTD mutant (gray line, p = 0.7; Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6E and Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: kd2 values for ΔCTD variants were, in general, lower than those of their CTD-containing counterparts.
source: kd2 values for ΔCTD variants were, in general, lower than those of their CTD-containing counterparts (Figure 6F), indicating the importance of the CTD for the catalytic activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6F.

claim: The importance of the CTD for catalytic activity is consistent with previous reports on RNE constructs based on the MTS.
source: These findings are consistent with previous reports on RNE constructs based on the MTS (Lopez et al., 1999; Leroy et al., 2002; Islam et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published studies (Lopez et al., 1999; Leroy et al., 2002; Islam et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2024).

claim: Among ΔCTD variants with different membrane motifs, point mutants F575E and F582E exhibited higher kd2 than the MTS-based variant.
source: Among ΔCTD variants with different membrane motifs, point mutants F575E and F582E (MB% = 91% and 67%, respectively; Appendix 1—figure 1) exhibited higher kd2 than the MTS-based variant, in agreement with the fact that completely cytoplasmic ΔMTS ΔCTD exhibited higher kd2 than the MTS-containing ΔCTD (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6F and Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The LacY2-based RNE variant, which diffuses faster than the MTS version, did not show a corresponding increase in kd2.
source: However, the LacY2-based RNE variant, which diffuses faster than the MTS version (Figure 5G), did not show a corresponding increase in kd2 (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6F and Figure 5G.

claim: LacY6 and LacY12 versions showed even lower kd2 than MTS-based RNE ΔCTD.
source: Plus, LacY6 and LacY12 versions showed even lower kd2 than MTS-based RNE ΔCTD.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The reduced kd2 caused by ΔCTD cannot be rescued by faster diffusion of membrane-bound RNE.
source: Overall, these results indicate that the reduced kd2 caused by ΔCTD cannot be rescued by faster diffusion of membrane-bound RNE.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective data on kd2 of various ΔCTD mutants.

claim: The reduced kd2 caused by ΔCTD may be further impaired by large and slow membrane motifs (such as LacY12).
source: In fact, it may be further impaired by large and slow membrane motifs (such as LacY12).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing lower kd2 for LacY12-based RNE ΔCTD.

claim: The presence of the CTD appears to buffer the effects of large membrane-binding motifs on RNE's catalytic activity, helping to maintain efficient post-transcriptional mRNA degradation (kd2).
source: The presence of the CTD appears to buffer the effects of large membrane-binding motifs on RNE's catalytic activity, helping to maintain efficient post-transcriptional mRNA degradation (kd2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that kd2 does not vary significantly across membrane-targeting variants when the CTD is present.

claim: The sequestration of RNE on the membrane confers the spatial and temporal separation between synthesis and decay of mRNAs.
source: Our study establishes the membrane enrichment and slow diffusion of RNE in E. coli. This supports the notion that sequestration of RNE on the membrane confers the spatial and temporal separation between synthesis and decay of mRNAs (Kim et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent study (Kim et al., 2024).

claim: The processing of rRNA and tRNA and small RNA-based gene regulations mediated by RNE likely take place on the membrane.
source: Furthermore, the processing of rRNA (Apirion, 1978; Bessarab et al., 1998; Ghora and Apirion, 1978; Li et al., 1999; Roy et al., 1983) and tRNA (Li and Deutscher, 2002; Ow and Kushner, 2002) and small RNA-based gene regulations (Ikeda et al., 2011; Reyer et al., 2021) mediated by RNE likely take place on the membrane.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the membrane localization of RNE and supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: The MB% of RNE measured in this study (93%) is close to 91% previously reported using immunogold labeling and freeze-fracture electron microscopy.
source: For WT RNE, our analysis showed MB% of 93%, close to 91% previously reported using immunogold labeling and freeze-fracture electron microscopy (Liou et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Liou et al., 2001).

claim: The MTS segment exhibited a reduction in MB% from 100% to 83% when cells were grown in M9 minimal medium with succinate as the sole carbon source without supplements.
source: The MTS segment exhibited a reduction in MB% from 100% to 83% (Appendix 1—figure 1), suggesting that MTS-mediated membrane binding can be sensitive to growth conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The MB% of WT RNE was only marginally affected by the media change to M9 minimal medium with succinate.
source: However, the MB% of WT RNE was only marginally affected by the same media change (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: Tetramer formation stabilizes RNE membrane localization, even when individual MTS motifs exhibit a weak membrane affinity.
source: We speculate that tetramer formation stabilizes RNE membrane localization, even when individual MTS motifs exhibit a weak membrane affinity.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculative explanation for the observed stability of WT RNE membrane localization.

claim: MinD becomes membrane-associated upon dimerization, indicating that oligomerization enhances the membrane binding of this peripheral membrane protein.
source: A similar phenomenon has been observed with MinD; although its amphipathic motif alone is cytoplasmic, MinD becomes membrane-associated upon dimerization, indicating that oligomerization enhances the membrane binding of this peripheral membrane protein (Szeto et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Szeto et al., 2003).

claim: The tetrameric structure of RNE may reinforce membrane association, buffering against changes in cellular metabolism or lipid environment that would otherwise weaken MTS-mediated binding.
source: By analogy, the tetrameric structure of RNE may reinforce membrane association, buffering against changes in cellular metabolism or lipid environment that would otherwise weaken MTS-mediated binding.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculative explanation by analogy to MinD.

claim: Individual TM motifs exhibited strong membrane association regardless of growth conditions.
source: While individual TM motifs exhibited strong membrane association regardless of growth conditions (Appendix 1—figure 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: LacY2-based RNE can lose membrane-binding affinity, unlike MTS-based RNE.
source: we found LacY2-based RNE can lose membrane-binding affinity, unlike MTS-based RNE.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The loss of MB% in LacY2-based RNE was observed only in the presence of the CTD.
source: The loss of MB% in LacY2-based RNE was observed only in the presence of the CTD (Appendix 1—figure 1), suggesting that the CTD negatively affects membrane binding of RNE, possibly by altering protein conformation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: All ΔCTD RNE mutants tested exhibited higher MB% than their CTD-containing counterparts.
source: In fact, all ΔCTD RNE mutants we tested exhibited higher MB% than their CTD-containing counterparts (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: WT RNE (containing CTD) showed an MB% of 93%, whereas its ΔCTD version, RNE (1–592), showed 100%.
source: For example, WT RNE (containing CTD) showed an MB% of 93%, whereas its ΔCTD version, RNE (1–592), showed 100%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The chimeric RNE-LacY6-CTD showed an MB% of 86%, while its ΔCTD version showed 100%.
source: Similarly, the chimeric RNE-LacY6-CTD showed an MB% of 86%, while its ΔCTD version showed 100% (Figure 5E, F; Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5E, F, and Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The CTD's effect on decreasing membrane association may be related to the CTD's role in promoting phase-separated ribonucleoprotein condensates, as observed in Caulobacter crescentus.
source: We speculate that this effect may be related to the CTD's role in promoting phase-separated ribonucleoprotein condensates, as observed in Caulobacter crescentus (Al-Husini et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculative explanation supported by a citation to a published study (Al-Husini et al., 2018).

claim: In E. coli, a modest increase in the clustering tendency of RNE was observed compared to ΔCTD.
source: In E. coli, we also observed a modest increase in the clustering tendency of RNE compared to ΔCTD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The DRNE measured in E. coli (0.018 μm2/s) is comparable to those measured in other bacterial species.
source: The DRNE we measured in E. coli (0.018 μm2/s) is comparable to those measured in other bacterial species.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with data from other bacterial species.

claim: In C. crescentus, the D of its cytoplasmic RNE was shown to be about 0.03 μm2/s.
source: For example, in C. crescentus, the D of its cytoplasmic RNE was shown to be about 0.03 μm2/s (Bayas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Bayas et al., 2018).

claim: The diffusion of RNase Y in B. subtilis was found in either a slow (0.031 μm2/s) or fast (0.3 μm2/s) population.
source: The diffusion of RNase Y in B. subtilis was found in either a slow (0.031 μm2/s) or fast (0.3 μm2/s) population (Oviedo-Bocanegra et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Oviedo-Bocanegra et al., 2021).

claim: The slow population of RNase Y in B. subtilis corresponds to RNase Y bound to mRNA and/or the putative RNA degradosome and the fast population represents freely diffusing RNase Y.
source: with the slow population corresponding to RNase Y bound to mRNA and/or the putative RNA degradosome and the fast population representing freely diffusing RNase Y.
evidence: The claim is presented as an interpretation of the two-population diffusion data for RNase Y.

claim: A two-population fit of the D histogram based on MB% identified the slow and fast subpopulations of E. coli RNE whose D values differed by a factor of 4.
source: In the case of E. coli RNE, a two-population fit of the D histogram based on MB% identified the slow and fast subpopulations whose D values differed by a factor of 4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two-population fit of E. coli RNE diffusion agrees with the finding that cytoplasmic RNE ΔMTS diffuses ~5 times as fast as WT RNE on average.
source: This agrees with our finding that cytoplasmic RNE ΔMTS diffuses ~5 times as fast as WT RNE on average (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: When cellular mRNAs were depleted by rifampicin treatment, RNE diffusion increased less than that of other RNA-binding proteins related to transcription and translation.
source: However, when cellular mRNAs were depleted by rifampicin treatment, RNE diffusion increased less than that of other RNA-binding proteins related to transcription and translation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The large and small ribosomal subunits, tRNA, and RNA polymerase showed a large (about 10- to 20-fold) increase in D upon rifampicin treatment.
source: For example, the large and small ribosomal subunits (Bakshi et al., 2012; Gray et al., 2019; Sanamrad et al., 2014), tRNA (Volkov et al., 2018), and RNA polymerase (Stracy et al., 2015) showed a large (about 10- to 20-fold) increase in D upon rifampicin treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Bakshi et al., 2012; Gray et al., 2019; Sanamrad et al., 2014; Volkov et al., 2018; Stracy et al., 2015).

claim: Hfq, an RNA chaperone involved in small RNA regulation together with RNE, showed a moderate increase (~2-fold) in D when RNA was depleted by rifampicin.
source: Interestingly, Hfq, an RNA chaperone involved in small RNA regulation together with RNE, showed a moderate increase (~2-fold) in D when RNA was depleted by rifampicin (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Park et al., 2021).

claim: The result on rifampicin effect on RNE diffusion is consistent with previous studies that examined the effect of rifampicin on RNE diffusion in E. coli as well as RNE in C. crescentus and RNase Y in B. subtilis.
source: We note that our result is consistent with previous studies that examined the effect of rifampicin on RNE diffusion in E. coli (Strahl et al., 2015; Hamouche et al., 2021) as well as RNE in C. crescentus (Bayas et al., 2018) and RNase Y in B. subtilis (Hamouche et al., 2020; Oviedo-Bocanegra et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Strahl et al., 2015; Hamouche et al., 2021; Bayas et al., 2018; Hamouche et al., 2020; Oviedo-Bocanegra et al., 2021).

claim: One possible explanation for the modest increase in RNE diffusion upon rifampicin treatment is that RNA-bound RNE (and RNase Y) is short-lived compared to the frame interval (~20 ms), unlike other RNA-binding proteins related to transcription and translation, interacting with RNA for ~1 min for elongation.
source: One possible explanation is that RNA-bound RNE (and RNase Y) is short-lived compared to our frame interval (~20 ms), unlike other RNA-binding proteins related to transcription and translation, interacting with RNA for ~1 min for elongation (Dai et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is presented as a possible explanation supported by a citation to a published study (Dai et al., 2016).

claim: The slow diffusion of the MTS in comparison to LacY2 and LacY6 suggests that MTS is less favorable for rapid lateral motion in the membrane.
source: Lastly, the slow diffusion of the MTS in comparison to LacY2 and LacY6 suggests that MTS is less favorable for rapid lateral motion in the membrane.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparative diffusion data.

claim: MD simulations demonstrated that the reduced diffusivity of the MTS may originate from a stronger interaction energy between the protein and the membrane.
source: Our MD simulations demonstrated that this reduced diffusivity may originate from a stronger interaction energy between the protein and the membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Whether the property of slower diffusion for peripheral motifs is specific to the MTS or generalizable to other peripheral versus integral membrane motifs remains to be tested.
source: Whether this property is specific to the MTS or generalizable to other peripheral versus integral membrane motifs remains to be tested.
evidence: The claim is presented as an open question for future research.

claim: Peripheral motifs interact with lipids orthogonally while integral membrane motifs align parallel to the bilayer and may diffuse more freely by coupling with the motion of surrounding lipids.
source: We speculate that this can be a general phenomenon, as peripheral motifs interact with lipids orthogonally while integral membrane motifs align parallel to the bilayer and may diffuse more freely by coupling with the motion of surrounding lipids.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculative explanation for the observed diffusion differences.

claim: The diffusion behavior of membrane-bound proteins reflects underlying protein–lipid interactions and membrane dynamics.
source: The diffusion behavior of membrane-bound proteins reflects underlying protein–lipid interactions and membrane dynamics (Knight et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Knight et al., 2010).

claim: Membrane-bound RNE lacking the CTD can stabilize mRNAs and increase protein expression.
source: For example, membrane-bound RNE lacking the CTD can stabilize mRNAs and increase protein expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that ΔCTD reduces kd2.

claim: This idea of using RNE lacking the CTD to increase protein expression has been used in a commercial E. coli BL21 strain (Invitrogen's One Shot BL21 Star) to increase recombinant protein yield.
source: This idea has been used in a commercial E. coli BL21 strain (Invitrogen's One Shot BL21 Star) to increase recombinant protein yield (Lopez et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Lopez et al., 1999).

claim: RNE variants with environmentally responsive MB%, such as RNE-LacY2-CTD, could be harnessed to tune mRNA half-lives and protein expression levels under different growth conditions.
source: Additionally, RNE variants with environmentally responsive MB%, such as RNE-LacY2-CTD, could be harnessed to tune mRNA half-lives and protein expression levels under different growth conditions.
evidence: The claim is presented as a potential application based on the findings of the study.
